title: Jude, Peter and the Spirits in Prison
bigQuestion: What did New Testament writers take from the story of the Watchers, and how have readers made sense of it?

story.title: Two Books on One Shelf
story.kicker: An imagined monk in Ethiopia copies the Letter of Jude and knows that the book Jude quotes is sitting right beside him.
paragraphs: Picture a monastery in the highlands of Ethiopia, several hundred years ago. Morning light comes through a small window. A monk sits on a low stool with a sheet of parchment across his knees. He dips a reed pen into black ink and copies the Letter of Jude, one of the shortest books of the New Testament. He writes in Ge'ez, the old church language of Ethiopia.

He reaches verse 14. Jude writes that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, spoke a prophecy about the Lord coming with thousands of his holy ones. The monk pauses. He knows those words. On the shelf behind him is another manuscript, the Book of Enoch, also in Ge'ez. Its very first chapter holds the same prophecy that Jude repeats.

For this monk, there is nothing strange about the match. His church, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, counts the Book of Enoch as part of its Bible. For most churches in Europe, the Middle East and the Americas, the story went another way. They kept Jude and set Enoch aside. For centuries, many Western readers knew Enoch's book only by name.

Jude is not the only New Testament writer who seems to know the Enoch story. Second Peter mentions angels who sinned and were held in chains. First Peter mentions spirits in prison from the days of Noah. In this chapter you will read these passages closely. You will see how Michael Heiser read them in light of 1 Enoch, and how other readers have read them differently.
story.think: Why might it matter that one church kept the Book of Enoch in its Bible while most others did not?

lessons.title: A Short, Urgent Letter
lessons.mainIdea: Jude is a 25-verse letter that warns a community about false teachers, using examples from old stories of judgment.
reading: The *Letter of Jude* sits just before Revelation at the end of the New Testament. It has only 25 verses. The writer calls himself Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James (Jude 1). Christian tradition has often identified him with Jude, or Judas, named in Mark 6:3 as a brother of Jesus. Some scholars accept that tradition, and others think a later writer used Jude's name. The date is also debated.

Jude says he meant to write about the salvation his readers shared. Instead, he felt he had to warn them. Certain people had slipped into the community, he says, and were turning grace into an excuse for wrong living (Jude 3–4). To make his point, Jude reaches for well-known stories of judgment. He names Israel in the wilderness, the angels who left their place, and Sodom and Gomorrah (Jude 5–7).

Many of Jude's examples come from the Hebrew Bible. Some do not. In verse 9 he mentions the archangel Michael arguing with the devil over the body of Moses. That scene is not in the Hebrew Bible. Early church writers said it came from a Jewish book about Moses that survives only in part. In verses 14–15, Jude quotes the Book of Enoch. Jude clearly expected his readers to know these stories too. This makes Jude a window into the wider library of *Second Temple* Jewish writings.

words.d: a 25-verse New Testament letter warning a community about false teachers
the period of Jewish history from about 516 BCE to 70 CE, when the rebuilt temple stood in Jerusalem
a chief angel; Jude 9 gives this title to Michael

look.title: Jude's Three Examples
look.text: Jude 5–7 lists three examples in a row. First, the people God brought out of Egypt, some of whom did not trust him. Second, angels who did not keep their own position and left their proper home. Third, Sodom and Gomorrah and the towns around them.
look.prompt: What do these three examples have in common? Why might a writer group them together when warning a community?

check.q: How long is the Letter of Jude?
check.why: Jude is one of the shortest books of the New Testament, with only 25 verses in a single chapter.

check.q: According to Jude 3–4, why did Jude write his letter?
choices: To tell the story of Jesus's birth
To explain how to build a temple
To warn about people turning grace into an excuse for wrong living
To give a list of the kings of Israel
check.why: Jude says he wanted to write about salvation but felt he had to warn his readers about false teachers.

check.q: Which example in Jude does NOT come from the Hebrew Bible?
choices: Michael arguing with the devil over the body of Moses
The people who did not trust God in the wilderness
check.why: Jude 9 draws on a Jewish tradition about Moses that is not found in the Hebrew Bible.

lessons.title: The Seventh from Adam
lessons.mainIdea: Jude calls Enoch 'the seventh from Adam', the same way Genesis 5 and 1 Enoch count his place in the family line.
reading: Jude 14 introduces its quotation with a title: Enoch, the seventh from Adam. That title comes from a count. *Genesis 5* lists the family line from Adam to Noah. If you count Adam as the first, Enoch is the seventh name: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared and Enoch. Ancient readers often counted this way, and the number seven had a sense of completeness in many biblical texts.

Genesis gives Enoch only a few verses, but they are unusual. Every other man in the list lives, has children and dies. Enoch lives 365 years, and then the text says he walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Genesis 5:24). The chapter does not say that Enoch died. Readers have wondered about that line for more than two thousand years.

Jewish writers in the Second Temple period filled in the gaps. The book we now call *1 Enoch* presents itself as Enoch's own words. It tells of journeys through heaven and of messages he carried. First Enoch also calls him the seventh from Adam (for example, 1 Enoch 60:8). When Jude uses the same title, he is speaking the language of that tradition. Heiser pointed to this as one of several signs that Jude knew 1 Enoch well.

words.d: the chapter listing the family line from Adam to Noah, with ages
an ancient Jewish book written in Enoch's name, parts of it from around the 3rd century BCE
the seventh from Adam in Genesis 5, who walked with God and was taken by God

look.title: Counting from Adam to Enoch
look.prompt: Using the list, explain why Jude can call Enoch 'the seventh from Adam'. What would change if you did not count Adam?

check.q: Where does the title 'the seventh from Adam' come from?
choices: Counting the family line in Genesis 5, starting with Adam
Counting the days of creation in Genesis 1
check.why: Genesis 5 lists Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared and Enoch, so Enoch is seventh.

check.q: What is unusual about Enoch in Genesis 5?
choices: The text does not say he died; it says God took him
He is the father of Adam
He is the oldest man in the list
check.why: Genesis 5:24 says Enoch walked with God and was not, for God took him.

check.q: Why did Heiser see Jude's title for Enoch as important?
choices: It shows Jude had never read Genesis
1 Enoch uses the same title, a sign that Jude knew that book
It was a title only used for kings
check.why: First Enoch also calls Enoch the seventh from Adam, so Jude is using the language of the Enoch tradition.

lessons.title: A Prophecy from 1 Enoch 1:9
lessons.mainIdea: Jude 14–15 repeats a prophecy that closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9, the clearest New Testament quotation of a book outside most Bibles.
reading: Put Jude 14–15 beside 1 Enoch 1:9 and the match is plain. Both say the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones. Both say he comes to carry out judgment on all. Both say he will convict the ungodly of their ungodly deeds and of the harsh words they have spoken against him. The order and the repeated word 'ungodly' line up closely.

Most scholars agree that Jude is quoting 1 Enoch, not just an idea from the air. The opening chapters of 1 Enoch survive in Aramaic fragments from the *Dead Sea Scrolls*, in Greek, and in full in Ge'ez. Jude's wording is closest to the Greek, though scholars still discuss exactly which form of the text he knew. The key point is simple: Jude introduces the words with 'Enoch prophesied'.

Readers have handled this in different ways. Heiser took it seriously. He argued that Jude and other New Testament writers treated 1 Enoch as a respected guide to Genesis 6, even though Jude does not call it Scripture. Some Christian readers think Jude quoted a true saying preserved in the book, without approving the whole book. Others say Jude simply used a text his readers valued. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads the match as support for 1 Enoch's place in its canon.

words.d: words repeated from another text, often with a signal such as 'as it says'
ancient Jewish manuscripts found near Qumran from 1947 to 1956, including Aramaic copies of parts of 1 Enoch
the ancient church language of Ethiopia, the only language in which all of 1 Enoch survives

look.title: Jude Names Enoch
look.text: And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, To execute judgment upon all, and to convince all that are ungodly among them of all their ungodly deeds which they have ungodly committed.
look.cite: Jude 14–15, King James Version (1611); compare 1 Enoch 1:9 in R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917)
look.prompt: Count how many times a form of 'ungodly' appears. What does the repetition add? What words in the verse tell you Jude is quoting someone?

check.q: Which passage in 1 Enoch does Jude 14–15 closely match?
check.why: Jude 14–15 closely matches the prophecy in 1 Enoch 1:9, near the start of the Book of the Watchers.

check.q: In which language does all of 1 Enoch survive?
check.why: Parts survive in Aramaic and Greek, but the complete book survives only in Ge'ez, the church language of Ethiopia.

check.q: How did Heiser read Jude's quotation of 1 Enoch?
choices: As a mistake that Jude later took back
As a quotation from Paul's letters
As proof that Jude wrote 1 Enoch himself
As a sign that New Testament writers respected 1 Enoch as a guide to Genesis 6
check.why: Heiser argued that Jude and others treated 1 Enoch as a respected guide to Genesis 6, though Jude does not call it Scripture.

lessons.title: Angels Who Left Their Place
lessons.mainIdea: Jude 6 speaks of angels who left their proper home and are kept in chains until judgment, echoing the Watchers of 1 Enoch.
reading: Jude 6 describes a group of angels. They did not keep their first position, or rule, and they left their own home. So they are kept in everlasting chains under darkness until the judgment of the great day. The verse is short, but every phrase counts. The Greek word for 'first estate' can mean an original rank or domain. The 'habitation' is their proper dwelling place.

Genesis 6:1–4 tells of the sons of God taking human wives. It says nothing about chains or darkness. First Enoch fills in that part. In 1 Enoch 10, God tells the angel Raphael to bind Azazel and put him in darkness. He tells Michael to bind Semjaza and his companions under the earth until the day of their judgment. These leaders of the *Watchers* are held, not destroyed.

Heiser argued that Jude 6 points straight to this Enoch story. Jude 7 supports the link, he noted. It says Sodom and Gomorrah sinned 'in like manner' and went after 'strange flesh'. Heiser read that as a comparison with angels crossing the line between heaven and earth. Other readers see Jude 6 as a general reference to angels who rebelled, perhaps at the beginning, with no link to Genesis 6. Both readings are held by serious scholars.

words.d: in 1 Enoch, heavenly beings who came down to earth and did wrong; the name comes from Daniel 4, where it is used for holy ones
the King James wording in Jude 6 for the angels' original rank or domain
in 1 Enoch 10, a leader of the Watchers whom Raphael binds and places in darkness

look.title: Jude 6
look.text: And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.
look.prompt: List the three things this verse says about the angels. Which of them can you also find in the 1 Enoch 10 account, and which only in Jude?

check.q: According to Jude 6, where are the angels kept?
check.why: Jude 6 says they are kept in everlasting chains under darkness until the judgment of the great day.

check.q: Which book tells of Raphael binding Azazel and Michael binding Semjaza?
check.why: 1 Enoch 10 gives these orders; Genesis 6 does not mention chains or darkness.

check.q: What verse did Heiser use to support linking Jude 6 with the Watchers story?
choices: Jude 7, which says Sodom sinned 'in like manner'
check.why: Heiser noted that Jude 7 compares Sodom's sin with the angels', which fits crossing the line between heaven and earth.

lessons.title: Tartarus in 2 Peter
lessons.mainIdea: Second Peter 2:4 uses a Greek verb built on Tartarus, the underworld prison where Greek stories said the Titans were held.
reading: Second Peter 2:4 says God did not spare the angels who sinned. The King James Version says God cast them down to hell and handed them over to chains of darkness until judgment. The English word 'hell' hides something. The Greek verb is *tartaroō*, which means 'to put in Tartarus'. It appears only here in the whole New Testament.

*Tartarus* was a well-known word to Greek speakers. In the poet Hesiod's Theogony, written about 700 BCE, Tartarus is a deep, dark place far below the earth. There the Titans, an older generation of gods, were locked up after losing a great war. So when 2 Peter uses this word, Greek-speaking readers would hear the idea of a prison for defeated divine beings, not a place for dead humans.

Heiser argued that the writer chose this word on purpose. He also pointed out that the Greek text of 1 Enoch 20:2 uses Tartarus too, naming the angel Uriel as set over it. For Heiser, 2 Peter is using a word both Greek and Jewish readers would link with imprisoned rebel beings. Other scholars agree the word is borrowed but say it may simply mean 'the lowest depths', without any intended link to the Titans.

words.d: a Greek verb meaning 'to put in Tartarus', found in the New Testament only at 2 Peter 2:4
in Greek stories, a deep prison under the earth where the Titans were held
in Greek stories such as Hesiod's Theogony, an older generation of gods defeated and locked in Tartarus

look.title: 2 Peter 2:4
look.text: For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment;
look.cite: 2 Peter 2:4, King James Version (1611); 'cast them down to hell' translates the Greek tartaroō
look.prompt: Compare this verse with Jude 6. What words or ideas do the two verses share? What does 2 Peter add?

check.q: What does the Greek verb tartaroō mean?
check.why: Tartaroō means 'to put in Tartarus'. The King James Version translates it 'cast them down to hell'.

check.q: In Hesiod's Theogony, who were held in Tartarus?
check.why: Hesiod, about 700 BCE, tells of the Titans being locked in Tartarus after losing a war.

check.q: Which Jewish text did Heiser note also uses the word Tartarus in its Greek form?
check.why: The Greek text of 1 Enoch 20:2 names Uriel as the angel set over Tartarus.

lessons.title: Angels, Noah, then Sodom
lessons.mainIdea: Second Peter 2:4–8 lists judgments in the same order as Genesis, which many readers take as a sign the angels' sin is the one in Genesis 6.
reading: Read 2 Peter 2:4–8 as a list. First come the angels who sinned (verse 4). Next comes the flood in the days of Noah, when God kept Noah and seven others safe (verse 5). Then come Sodom and Gomorrah, and the rescue of Lot (verses 6–8). The writer uses these examples to show that God knows how to rescue the faithful and hold the wrong-doers for judgment (verse 9).

Look at the order. In Genesis, the sons of God story (Genesis 6:1–4) comes right before the flood (Genesis 6–9). Sodom comes later (Genesis 19). Second Peter follows the same sequence. Heiser and many other scholars take this as a clue. If the angels' sin sits just before Noah in the list, it is most likely the sin of Genesis 6, as 1 Enoch tells it.

Other readers disagree. A long Christian tradition links the fall of angels with a rebellion led by Satan before the creation of humans, or around the time of Eden. In that reading, 2 Peter 2:4 refers to that early fall, and the order of the list is not meant to point to Genesis 6. Readers of both views agree that 2 Peter uses the angels, the flood and Sodom as warnings and as signs of rescue.

words.d: the order in which things come one after another
the great water in Genesis 6–9 from which Noah and his family were kept safe in the ark
the idea that some angels turned against God; readers place it at different times

look.title: Two Lists Side by Side
look.text: Genesis: sons of God and human wives (6:1–4); the flood and Noah (6–9); Sodom and Lot (19). Second Peter 2: angels who sinned (2:4); the flood and Noah (2:5); Sodom and Lot (2:6–8).
look.prompt: What does the matching order suggest? What would a reader who places the angels' fall before Eden say about the same list?

check.q: What three examples appear in 2 Peter 2:4–8, in order?
choices: Angels who sinned, the flood in Noah's days, Sodom and Gomorrah
check.why: Second Peter lists the angels (2:4), then Noah and the flood (2:5), then Sodom and Lot (2:6–8).

check.q: Why do Heiser and many scholars link 2 Peter 2:4 with Genesis 6?
choices: The angels come right before Noah, the same order as in Genesis
2 Peter quotes Genesis 6:4 word for word
check.why: The sons of God story comes right before the flood in Genesis, and 2 Peter keeps that order.

check.q: How does another long Christian tradition read the angels' sin in 2 Peter 2:4?
choices: As an early rebellion led by Satan, before or around the time of Eden
As a story about Roman soldiers
As the golden calf at Sinai
As the building of the tower of Babel
check.why: Many Christians have placed the fall of angels at an early rebellion, not at Genesis 6.

lessons.title: A Famous Hard Passage
lessons.mainIdea: First Peter 3:18–22 says Christ went and preached to spirits in prison who disobeyed in Noah's day, one of the hardest passages in the New Testament.
reading: First Peter was written to Christians who were being treated badly for their faith. In chapter 3, the writer encourages them with Christ's example. Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring people to God (3:18). He was put to death in the flesh but made alive in the Spirit. Then comes a surprise in verses 19–20.

In the Spirit, the text says, Christ went and preached to the *spirits in prison*. These spirits had disobeyed long ago, when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. Only eight people were saved through water. Verse 21 links that water to baptism. Verse 22 ends with Christ in heaven at God's right hand, with angels, authorities and powers made subject to him.

Readers have argued over these verses for a very long time. Who are the spirits? Where is the prison? When did Christ go there, and what did he preach? The Greek verb is *kēryssō*, which means to announce or proclaim. It does not always mean preaching a message of rescue. Keep these four questions in mind. The next two lessons look at three main answers.

words.d: the phrase in 1 Peter 3:19 for beings Christ preached to, linked with disobedience in Noah's day
a Greek verb meaning to announce or proclaim, like a herald
the Christian washing with water; 1 Peter 3:21 compares it to the water of Noah's flood

look.title: 1 Peter 3:19–20
look.text: By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison; Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.
look.prompt: Underline the words that tell you when these spirits disobeyed. Why might a reader who knows 1 Enoch think of the Watchers here?

check.q: According to 1 Peter 3:20, when did the spirits in prison disobey?
choices: In the days of Noah, while the ark was being built
During the time of the judges
check.why: First Peter 3:20 places their disobedience in the days of Noah, while God waited and the ark was built.

check.q: What does the Greek verb kēryssō mean?
check.why: Kēryssō means to announce like a herald; it does not always mean preaching a message of rescue.

check.q: What does 1 Peter 3:22 say about angels, authorities and powers?
choices: They wrote the Book of Enoch
They are made subject to Christ
check.why: Verse 22 says Christ is at God's right hand, with angels, authorities and powers made subject to him.

lessons.title: Heiser's Reading Through Enoch
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser, with many scholars, read the spirits in prison as the Watchers, and Christ's preaching as an announcement of victory over them.
reading: In 1 Enoch 12–16, the Watchers are already bound. They ask Enoch to carry a written request to God, hoping for forgiveness. Enoch goes, and he returns with God's answer. They will have no peace, and their request is refused. In that story, a righteous man goes to imprisoned spirits and announces God's verdict on them.

Heiser argued that 1 Peter 3 draws on this story, as he explains in The Unseen Realm (2015) and Reversing Hermon (2017). The spirits in prison are the Watchers who sinned before the flood. Christ, like a new Enoch, goes to them and announces that he has won. They are not given a second chance. Verse 22 then shows the result: angels, authorities and powers are placed under Christ. This reading was also argued in detail by the Catholic scholar William J. Dalton in a 1965 study.

This reading explains some puzzling details. The New Testament usually uses 'spirits' for non-human beings rather than for dead people. It explains why Noah is mentioned and why the passage ends with powers made subject. Heiser saw it as a picture of what he called Christ's mission to reclaim what the rebel powers had taken. Critics of this reading ask why Peter did not name Enoch or the Watchers if he meant them.

words.d: a judge's final decision
the chapters in which Enoch carries the bound Watchers' request to God and brings back a refusal
a public announcement, such as a king's victory or a court's decision

look.title: Two Announcements
look.text: In 1 Enoch 12–16, Enoch goes to the bound Watchers and announces that their request is refused. In 1 Peter 3:19–22, Christ goes to spirits in prison from Noah's days and proclaims; afterward angels, authorities and powers are subject to him.
look.prompt: List two ways these two scenes are alike and one way they differ. How strong do you think the link is, and why?

check.q: In 1 Enoch 12–16, what message does Enoch bring back to the Watchers?
choices: They are forgiven and set free
Their request is refused and they will have no peace
check.why: In 1 Enoch 12–16, the Watchers' request for forgiveness is refused.

check.q: According to Heiser, who are the spirits in prison in 1 Peter 3:19?
choices: The Watchers who sinned before the flood
check.why: Heiser read the spirits in prison as the Watchers of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch.

check.q: Which scholar argued for a similar reading in a 1965 study?
check.why: The Catholic scholar William J. Dalton argued in 1965 that Christ proclaimed victory to imprisoned spirits.

lessons.title: Two Other Main Readings
lessons.mainIdea: Other readers say Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day, or that Christ went to the realm of the dead after his death.
reading: One reading comes from Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, who wrote about it in a letter in the early 400s. He thought the preaching happened in Noah's own time. Christ, by his Spirit, spoke through Noah to the people of that day. They did not listen, and so they are now 'in prison'. Some later Protestant scholars have followed this reading, which does not need 1 Enoch at all.

A second reading is often called the *harrowing of hell*. Here, between his death and resurrection, Christ went down to the realm of the dead. There he announced the good news to the people who had died, including those of Noah's time. Readers often point to 1 Peter 4:6, which says the gospel was preached to the dead. The Apostles' Creed says Christ 'descended into hell', which many churches understand in this way. Eastern Orthodox icons of the resurrection often show Christ pulling Adam and Eve from their graves.

So there are three main readings: preaching through Noah, preaching to the dead, and proclaiming victory to the Watchers. Each has strong points and hard questions. Scholars still disagree, and all three are held by careful readers today. Knowing all three helps you see why 1 Peter 3 is called one of the hardest passages in the New Testament.

words.d: a bishop in North Africa (354–430 CE) whose writings shaped Western Christianity
the belief that Christ went to the realm of the dead after his death and freed or preached to people there
an early Christian statement of belief still used in many Western churches

look.title: Three Readings in a Row
look.text: Reading A: Christ's Spirit spoke through Noah to people of his day. Reading B: after his death, Christ went to the realm of the dead and preached to people there. Reading C: Christ proclaimed his victory to the imprisoned Watchers of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch.
look.prompt: For each reading, answer: who are the spirits, and when did Christ go to them? Which detail in 1 Peter 3:18–22 does each reading explain best?

check.q: In Augustine's reading, when did the preaching to the spirits happen?
choices: In Noah's own time, through Noah
At the end of the world
check.why: Augustine held that Christ's Spirit spoke through Noah to people of his day, who are now in prison.

check.q: What does the phrase 'harrowing of hell' refer to?
choices: The belief that Christ went to the realm of the dead and preached or freed people there
The binding of Azazel in 1 Enoch
A Greek story about the Titans
check.why: The harrowing of hell is the belief that Christ went to the dead between his death and resurrection.

check.q: Which verse do readers of the harrowing-of-hell view often point to?
choices: 1 Peter 4:6, the gospel preached to the dead
check.why: First Peter 4:6 says the gospel was preached to the dead, which supports that reading.

lessons.title: Why Some Doubted Jude
lessons.mainIdea: Some early Christians hesitated to accept Jude because it quoted 1 Enoch, but churches kept Jude in their Bibles.
reading: A *canon* is the list of books a community treats as its Scripture. The New Testament canon took shape over several centuries. Some books were accepted early and almost everywhere. Others were questioned for a time. Jude was one of the questioned books. So were 2 Peter, James, 2 and 3 John and Revelation, for different reasons.

Eusebius, a church historian writing about 325 CE, grouped Jude among the 'disputed' books. They were known and read by many, but not accepted by everyone. Jerome, the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin, wrote in 393 CE that many rejected Jude because it quoted Enoch, a book not in Scripture. He added that Jude had gained authority by its age and use, and was counted with the holy books.

In the end, Jude stayed in the New Testament of every major church. Most churches did not add 1 Enoch. Heiser pointed out that this history shows a tension. Early readers noticed that Jude valued Enoch's book, and that bothered some of them. Yet they kept Jude. For Heiser, that makes 1 Enoch important for reading the New Testament, whether or not a church counts it as Scripture.

words.d: the list of books a community treats as its Scripture
books that early Christians knew but did not all accept, such as Jude and 2 Peter
a Christian scholar (c. 347–420 CE) who translated the Bible into Latin

look.title: Jerome on Jude
look.text: Jude, the brother of James, left a short letter. Because it uses a quotation from the Book of Enoch, which is not counted as Scripture, many people reject it. Even so, it has earned its authority through long use, and it is counted among the holy writings.
look.cite: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 4, 393 CE (paraphrased in plain English)
look.prompt: What reason does Jerome give for why some rejected Jude? What reason does he give for why it was accepted anyway?

check.q: What is a canon?
choices: The list of books a community treats as its Scripture
check.why: A canon is the list of books a community accepts as Scripture.

check.q: According to Jerome, why did many people reject Jude?
choices: It quoted the Book of Enoch
check.why: Jerome wrote in 393 CE that many rejected Jude because it quoted Enoch.

check.q: How did Eusebius classify Jude around 325 CE?
choices: As a forgery to be burned
As the first book of the New Testament
As a book of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: Eusebius listed Jude among the disputed books: known and read, but not accepted by all.

lessons.title: Enoch In and Out of the Bible
lessons.mainIdea: Quoting a book does not make it Scripture for most churches, but the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches include 1 Enoch in their canon.
reading: Quoting a book is not the same as calling it Scripture. Paul quotes Greek poets in Acts 17:28 and Titus 1:12, yet no church put those poets in the Bible. Many readers apply the same rule to Jude and 1 Enoch. Others note that Jude says Enoch 'prophesied', a word he does not use lightly. Around 200 CE, the North African writer Tertullian argued that the Book of Enoch should be respected, partly because Jude quotes it.

Judaism did not include 1 Enoch in the Hebrew Bible, and most churches followed. The Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Protestant canons all leave it out. The *Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church* and the Eritrean Orthodox Church are different. Their canon includes 1 Enoch, and Jubilees as well. That is why the full text survived in Ge'ez, copied by hand in monasteries for centuries.

In 1773 the Scottish traveler James Bruce brought Ge'ez copies of 1 Enoch to Europe. English translations followed, including R. H. Charles's in 1917. Then the Dead Sea Scrolls showed that Jews in the Second Temple period had read Enoch in Aramaic. Heiser used all this evidence. He did not argue that 1 Enoch belongs in every Bible. He argued that readers need it to understand how the New Testament writers read Genesis 6.

words.d: the ancient church of Ethiopia, whose canon includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees
a Christian writer from North Africa, about 200 CE, who argued that the Book of Enoch should be respected
an ancient Jewish retelling of Genesis and part of Exodus, in the Ethiopian Orthodox canon

look.title: The Five Parts of 1 Enoch
look.cite: Standard division of 1 Enoch; R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (1917)
look.prompt: Jude quotes chapter 1. Which part is that, and which part is the longest? Why might the Watchers part matter most for this chapter?

check.q: Which churches include 1 Enoch in their canon?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches
check.why: Only the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Church include 1 Enoch in their Bibles.

check.q: What example shows that quoting a book does not always make it Scripture?
choices: Paul quotes Greek poets in Acts 17:28 and Titus 1:12
check.why: Paul quotes Greek poets, yet no church added those poets to its Bible.

check.q: What did Heiser argue about 1 Enoch?
choices: It is the same book as Jubilees
Readers need it to understand how New Testament writers read Genesis 6
Every church must add it to the Bible
It was written after the New Testament
check.why: Heiser argued 1 Enoch is needed to understand New Testament readings of Genesis 6, without claiming it belongs in every canon.

review.q: Which New Testament book directly quotes 1 Enoch 1:9?
review.why: Jude 14–15 quotes the prophecy of 1 Enoch 1:9 and names Enoch as its speaker.

review.q: Why is Enoch called 'the seventh from Adam'?
choices: He is seventh in the Genesis 5 family line, counting Adam
review.why: Genesis 5 lists Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch.

review.q: Which Greek word in 2 Peter 2:4 is built on the name of the Titans' prison?
review.why: Tartaroō means 'to put in Tartarus', the Greek prison of the Titans.

review.q: What do Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 both say about the angels who sinned?
choices: They are held in chains of darkness until judgment
review.why: Both verses describe the angels as kept in chains and darkness until judgment.

review.q: In 1 Peter 3:19–20, the spirits in prison are linked with which time?
review.why: First Peter 3:20 says they disobeyed in the days of Noah, while the ark was built.

review.q: Which reading of 1 Peter 3:19 says Christ spoke through Noah to people of his day?
review.why: Augustine held that Christ's Spirit preached through Noah to the people of that time.

review.q: How did Heiser connect 1 Peter 3 with 1 Enoch 12–16?
choices: Like Enoch, Christ goes to imprisoned spirits and announces God's verdict
Enoch builds the ark for Noah
Peter copies Enoch's list of angel names
review.why: Heiser saw Christ as a new Enoch, proclaiming victory to the imprisoned Watchers.

review.q: Why did some early Christians hesitate to accept the Letter of Jude?
choices: It quoted the Book of Enoch
It was longer than the Gospels
review.why: Jerome reported that many rejected Jude because it quoted Enoch, a book outside Scripture.
